community.guide.after.1: In the "Community access" card, turn on the community code. Set an expiry or a limit on sign-ups if you like.
community.guide.after.2: Use "Copy message" and send it. It contains the address and the code.
community.guide.after.3: Friends open the address, choose "I have a community code", enter the code, and pick a username and password.
community.guide.after.4: You see who joined under Users, and can remove anyone there. A new code stops the old one working; accounts already made stay.
community.guide.after.p: You can also make guest accounts yourself under Users and skip the code.
community.guide.choose.own: Your own address (for example servers.yourdomain.com): permanent, and the page updates live. It needs a free Cloudflare account and a domain whose DNS is managed by Cloudflare. If you don't have one, a domain costs a few dollars a year and can be added to Cloudflare for free. Then pick between a token (easiest) or a tunnel you already made on this PC.
community.guide.choose.temporary: A temporary link: no account, nothing to buy, ready in a minute. The address is random (something-words.trycloudflare.com) and changes each time the view starts, so you'd have to send friends a new one. The page refreshes every few seconds instead of live. Good for trying it, or for a one-off.
community.guide.existing.1: Make sure the address you want already points at that tunnel. In a terminal: cloudflared tunnel route dns servers.yourdomain.com (a one-time step, if it isn't done already).
community.guide.existing.2: Stop any other program already running that tunnel (for example one started by PM2, a Windows service or a script). If two programs run the same tunnel, Cloudflare splits visitors between them and about half will reach the wrong one. The card warns you if it sees this.
community.guide.existing.3: "Set up" → "My own address, using the tunnel already on this PC", enter the address, then "Turn it on".
community.guide.existing.after: GodlyPanel runs the tunnel with a settings file of its own that sends the address to the community view. It does not change your own settings file.
community.guide.existing.intro: This is for a tunnel made on the command line with cloudflared tunnel create. If you have one, "Set up" lists it. If you want a new one, the token route above is simpler.
community.guide.quick.1: Choose "Set up", let it download cloudflared if it asks, and pick "A temporary link".
community.guide.quick.2: Choose "Turn it on". After a few seconds the address appears in the card. Use "Copy".
community.guide.quick.3: Turn on the community code (the card below) and send the generated message to your friends.
community.guide.quick.after: If you turn it off and on again, or restart the panel, the address changes. The community code stays the same.
community.guide.safety.1: Only guests can sign in on the community view, and a guest can only read status. The panel itself refuses anything that arrives through a tunnel, so pointing a tunnel at the wrong place by mistake can't expose it.
community.guide.safety.2: Join passwords, admin passwords and server settings are never shown to guests. People who find the address can see that a sign-in page exists; they can't do anything without an account or the code.
community.guide.safety.3: "Turn off" stops the tunnel and closes the small server straight away. Turning off the community code stops new sign-ups but doesn't remove accounts that exist.

community.guide.title: Community view: guide
community.guide.token.1: Sign in at {link} (Cloudflare Zero Trust; the free plan is enough) and open Networks → Tunnels.
community.guide.token.2: Choose "Create a tunnel", type "Cloudflared", give it a name (for example "godlypanel"), and save.
community.guide.token.3: On the next page you'll see install commands for several systems. You don't run them: just copy the token, the very long text after --token (or after service install).
community.guide.token.4: Open the Public Hostname tab and add one: a subdomain and your domain (for example servers + yourdomain.com), service type HTTP, URL {url}. That number is the community view's own port, not the panel's.
community.guide.token.5: Back here: "Set up" → "My own address, with a tunnel from the Cloudflare dashboard". Paste the token and type the full address you just made (servers.yourdomain.com), then "Turn it on".
community.guide.token.after: The address you type must match the Public Hostname exactly. The community view only answers to that name.
community.guide.trouble.421: "This address isn't served here" (421). The name the visitor used isn't the one you entered in the set-up. Re-enter it exactly, or use the address the card shows.
community.guide.trouble.badGateway: The address shows "Bad gateway", error 1033 or 530. The tunnel isn't connected. Look at the card: it should say "On". Another copy of the same tunnel running elsewhere can also cause this.
community.guide.trouble.notFound: The address shows a plain "404" or a blank page. The address in Cloudflare doesn't match the one you entered here, or it points somewhere other than localhost:{port}. For a tunnel you already had, the address must be routed to that tunnel.
community.guide.trouble.port: "Port … is in use". Another program is using the community view's port. Choose another in the settings (it only matters on this PC).
community.guide.trouble.slow: Updates seem slow. On a temporary link the page checks every few seconds instead of live. A permanent address of your own updates live.
community.guide.trouble.someOnly: It works for some people and not others. Two programs are running the same tunnel; stop the other one.
community.guide.trouble.token: The token was refused. Copy it again from the tunnel's page in the Cloudflare dashboard; it is one long line.
community.guide.trouble.waiting: "Waiting for Cloudflare to give out the address" never ends. This PC couldn't reach Cloudflare. Check the internet connection, and that Windows Firewall or security software isn't blocking cloudflared (use "Details" in the card to see what it said).
community.guide.what.p1: The community view gives people outside your home one web address. They sign in as a guest (or make their own account with a community code) and see the dashboard: which servers are up, who is on, and how to join. That is all.
community.guide.what.p2: By default it is not your panel on the internet. It is a separate, much smaller page. Administrators and moderators can't sign in on it, and nothing can be started, stopped, edited or deleted through it. (If some of your staff are never on your home network, you can switch on Let administrators and moderators sign in here too. Then they get the whole panel through this address, so use long, unique passwords.) Your panel stays on your own network, and nothing is opened on your router: GodlyPanel makes an outbound connection to Cloudflare (a "tunnel"), and Cloudflare passes visitors back down it.
community.guide.what.p3: The tunnel is run by cloudflared, Cloudflare's own program. GodlyPanel starts it, keeps it running and stops it for you. Cloudflare can see the traffic that passes through its tunnel, as with any service of its kind.

create.askSteamBody: Games are installed with SteamCMD, Valve's official tool. It isn't included with GodlyPanel, so it will be downloaded once from Valve and kept with your data. Already have a copy? Cancel and point Settings at it instead.

create.askZipBody1: This game is not installed through SteamCMD. The panel will download it from the project's releases on GitHub:
create.askZipBody2: It is fetched over https from GitHub only, checked against the SHA-256 checksum GitHub publishes for it (a download without a matching checksum is thrown away), and unpacked only into this server's own folder. Nothing is downloaded until you press the button.
create.extraIntro.one: It also needs one more file that the download does not include, so the panel fetches it for you:
create.extraIntro.other: It also needs more files that the download does not include, so the panel fetches them for you:
create.extraSigned: Each is checked against a checksum built into the panel and must carry a valid {signers} signature, or it is thrown away. Nothing is installed on this PC: the panel only takes the needed files out and puts them in the server's own folder. By continuing you accept the licence that comes with {files}.

panelUpdate.checkedAgainst: It is checked against the checksum the release publishes, then GodlyPanel closes, swaps the files and starts the new version. That takes about half a minute.
panelUpdate.failedUndone: The update to {version} didn't work and was undone. {message}
panelUpdate.ifNotStart: If the new version doesn't start, the old one is put back automatically.
panelUpdate.keepRunningRest: , and your settings, accounts and backups are not touched. The panel itself is unavailable for those seconds: anyone using it is disconnected and the page reloads when it's back.
panelUpdate.notGoAhead: The update didn't go ahead: {error} Nothing was changed.
panelUpdate.onlyChanged: Only what changed is downloaded ({size}, not the whole package).
panelUpdate.overlayBody: This takes about half a minute. This page reloads by itself when GodlyPanel is back. Your game servers keep running.
panelUpdate.sigInvalid: This release's signature doesn't match, so the panel won't install it. It may have been changed after it was published. Don't use it, and tell the project.
panelUpdate.sigMissing: This release isn't signed by the project, so the panel won't install it by itself. Download it from the releases page only if you trust where it came from.
panelUpdate.sigNoChecksum: This release doesn't publish a checksum the panel can verify, so it won't install it by itself. Download the package and unzip it instead.
panelUpdate.signed: Signed by the project: the panel checked this update's signature before offering it.
panelUpdate.slow: This is taking longer than usual. If GodlyPanel doesn't come back, start it from its folder: if the new version can't start, the old one is put back automatically.
panelUpdate.title: GodlyPanel version
panelUpdate.unverified: The release notes gave no checksum to compare it with, so it is unverified.
panelUpdate.verifiedNotes: It matches the checksum in the release notes.
panelUpdate.verifiedSigned: It matches the checksum in the project's signed manifest.
panelUpdate.wholePackage: This version needs a newer Electron, so the whole package is downloaded ({size}).
